headline: Halfway Rock holds its cod on the turn, bass working the Harpswell ledges
subhead: Groundfish steady in deep water while striped bass and blues chase bait along the island edges on the moving tide.
body_markdown:
_AI fishing-intelligence report. It was prepared from 0 supplied evidence records and 17 supplied analysis inputs; it does not claim firsthand fishing._

There's a particular quiet that settles over Halfway Rock at the top of the tide — the swirl around its base goes still, the gulls stop working the rip, and for ten or fifteen minutes the whole ledge seems to hold its breath before the water starts moving the other way. I've watched that turn happen more times than I can count, and it's still the best classroom this bay has. This week, that slack window has been the tell for where the cod and haddock are sitting: tight to the rock's eastern face, in 80 to 110 feet, where the current sweeps bait against the granite and stacks it up before the tide reverses.

Groundfish have been steady out there, not spectacular, but honest. Diamond jigs — the heavier 6- to 8-ounce models — dropped straight down and worked in short lifts off bottom have been taking keeper cod in the mid-20-inch range, with the occasional haddock mixed in on the drift as the tide starts to build. The key has been fishing the last hour of the ebb into the first hour of flood, when the bait gets pinned against the ledge instead of scattered across open water. Anglers running bait — clams or herring chunks on a simple ledger rig — have done about as well as the jig crowd, which tells you the fish aren't picky right now, just concentrated.

Striped bass have settled into their August pattern along the Harpswell shoreline and the ledges off Bailey Island. Look for them working current seams in 15 to 30 feet on the last two hours of the flood, particularly where the tide sweeps around points and drops bait into deeper pockets. Live mackerel, when you can find them, remain the gold standard here, but the mackerel schools have thinned considerably since their May peak — this is typical for the season, not a red flag, just a sign the run has run its course for now. In their place, umbrella rigs and topwater plugs worked over visible bait have been producing better than static bait soak. Two Lights has been giving up bass on the outgoing tide as well, fish holding on the rockweed edges where the current pulls baitfish off the ledge.

Bluefish have shown up in decent numbers wherever bunker pods have concentrated, and the bite has been about what the pattern predicted — we flagged this a few weeks back, noting that wherever bait pods stack up under stable high-pressure weather, the topwater feeds tend to hold, and that's exactly what's played out around Peaks Island and the mouth of the Harraseeket. Poppers and 2-ounce metal, cast into visible surface commotion rather than blind-cast across open water, have connected consistently on blues in the 3- to 6-pound range. The stable weather window we've had has kept that pattern intact — no big fronts to scatter the bait, no dramatic temperature swings to push fish off structure.

One honest note: this hasn't been an easy-limits week. The groundfish bite requires patience and precise positioning on the ledge — drift off by fifty yards and the fish simply aren't there. The bass bite has been more about timing the tide correctly than covering water; anglers fishing the wrong stage have come back with little to show for a full afternoon. This is a bay that rewards study over volume, which suits my temperament, if not always the impatient angler's.

Cape Small has been quieter than the inner bay, which is not unusual for this time of year — the open coastal exposure there means bait gets pushed around more by wind and swell, and consistency suffers. If conditions stay settled, I'd expect that area to firm up as water temperatures hold steady through the week.

Looking ahead, the moon is moving toward the next quarter, which should keep tidal exchange moderate rather than extreme — good news for anyone working the ledges, since violent tidal swings tend to blow bait off structure before fish can organize on it. If the stable high-pressure pattern holds, as it has, expect the cod and haddock to keep sitting tight on Halfway Rock's structure through the week, and the bass and blues to keep working the same current seams around Harpswell, Bailey Island, and Peaks. If a front does push through and stirs things up, I'd shift attention to the more protected inner ledges — Bailey Island's lee side, in particular — where bait tends to hold even when the open water gets uncomfortable. Either way, fish the tide stages deliberately. This bay doesn't reward guesswork, but it rewards patience handsomely.
